post.title: Single Trunk Model Explained: Golden Branches, Feature Toggles, and Continuous Feature Delivery
post.subtitle: Why modern teams keep one golden branch releasable, ship behind toggles, and handle hotfixes without GitFlow drama.
post.brief: The single trunk model exists to reduce integration pain, shorten feedback loops, and keep one golden branch always releasable. Teams make it work with strong CI, short-lived feature branches, feature toggles, and a hotfix process that fixes trunk first instead of forking release history.

This walkthrough focuses on **Why the Single Trunk Model Exists at All**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Traditional branching models came from a reasonable instinct: isolate change so unfinished work does not break everyone else.
- The problem is that isolation solves one risk by creating three others.
- First, long-lived branches hide integration bugs until the most expensive moment, when several weeks of work collide with new trunk changes.

**Concepts in play:** canary-deployments, git-internals-and-versioning, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — Decision Matrix: When the Single Trunk Model Fits Best

- A lot of teams fail here because they ask, "Should we ban branches?" That is the wrong question.
- The right question is, "How quickly can unfinished work rejoin the main line safely?"

*Applies **canary-deployments** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The right question is, "How quickly can unfinished work rejoin the main line safely?"

## Stage 2 — The Core Vocabulary Teams Need to Agree On

- Before teams adapt this model, they need precise language.
- A lot of rollout confusion is really vocabulary confusion.
- Notice what is missing from that table: there is no rule saying feature branches are forbidden.
- Mature trunk teams still use them.

*Applies **git-internals-and-versioning** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Mature trunk teams still use them.

## Stage 3 — How Continuous Feature Delivery Works on One Branch

- The mechanics matter more than the slogan.
- A team cannot adopt a golden branch by declaring one.
- In practice, CFD on a single trunk usually works like this: 1.
- A developer starts work on a small change, often in a short-lived branch.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A developer starts work on a small change, often in a short-lived branch.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: How Teams Actually Adapt to a Golden Branch

- The cultural shift is usually harder than the Git change.
- The Internals Teams that succeed with a single trunk model usually redesign workflow in four internal layers.
- Merge policy becomes operational policy.
- Protected branch rules, mandatory checks, code owners, and fast review SLAs stop being optional hygiene and become release controls.

*Applies **canary-deployments** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Protected branch rules, mandatory checks, code owners, and fast review SLAs stop being optional hygiene and become release controls.

## Stage 5 — Visualizing the Flow from Commit to Hotfix

- The diagram below shows how a golden branch stays deployable while still allowing hidden work, gradual rollout, and urgent production repair.
- Read it left to right: work enters through a short-lived integration path, passes CI, lands on trunk, then gets exposed through toggles rather than branching history.
- The hotfix path loops back into the same trunk because the system stays maintainable only when one line of history remains authoritative.
- The important takeaway is that trunk remains the backbone of both normal delivery and incident response.

*Applies **git-internals-and-versioning** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Dev[Developer change] --> Branch[Short-lived feature branch]
    Branch --> Review[Review and CI gates]
    Review --> Trunk[Golden trunk branch]
    Trunk --> Toggle[Feature toggle default off]
    Toggle --> Deploy[Deployable artifact]
    Deploy --> Rollout[Progressive rollout]
    Incident[Production incident] --> Fix[Hotfix commit]
    Fix --> Review
    Fix --> Patch[Optional emergency patch from release tag]
    Patch --> Trunk
```

**Observable outcome:** The important takeaway is that trunk remains the backbone of both normal delivery and incident response.

## Stage 6 — How Different Teams Adapt the Model in Real Life

- A startup usually adopts this model first because speed hurts less when there is one place to integrate.
- Small teams can often begin with protected main, mandatory tests, and one simple feature flag service.
- A platform team adapts it differently.
- Their challenge is not only speed but coordination.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Their challenge is not only speed but coordination.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - The single trunk model exists to shrink integration risk, not to enforce a Git aesthetic.
- - A golden branch is only golden if CI and branch protection make it trustworthy.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.
